title: Discriminating Lindbladian Dynamics
authors: Robert Salzmann, Ludovico Lami, Martin B. Plenio, Susana F. Huelga
abstract: The fundamental task of quantum hypothesis testing, which consists in discriminating quantum objects, has been extensively studied for quantum states and channels. Here, we investigate the fundamental limits of discriminating an arbitrary pair of quantum Markovian dynamics generated by Lindbladians, focusing on the roles of total exposure time and temporal resolution. We allow adaptive choices of evolution durations and arbitrary instantaneous controls between them. We characterise the optimal type-II error exponent (Stein exponent) as the largest instantaneous increase of quantum relative entropy, and give an algebraic criterion for its finiteness in terms of the Lindbladians. Remarkably, an infinite exponent is equivalent to a vanishing type-II error probability at sufficiently large finite total time, for every positive type-I tolerance. While some dynamics admit a finite protocol with zero type-II error, others require increasingly fine temporal control. For the latter, the error vanishes as the minimum allowed evolution duration, or resolution time, tends to zero at fixed sufficiently large total time, but remains bounded away from zero at every fixed positive resolution time. We achieve this using quantum Zeno protocols, establishing temporal resolution as a resource for discrimination. When the null hypothesis is the identity semigroup, an infinite asymptotic error exponent has a stronger consequence: at a fixed finite total exposure time, the type-II error can be made arbitrarily small while keeping the type-I error exactly zero. This is impossible in the corresponding classical setting. Discriminating the identity semigroup from generalised amplitude damping on a qubit provides examples of all three regimes: a finite asymptotic error exponent, zero type-II error attainable at positive resolution time, and vanishing type-II error requiring the resolution time to tend to zero.
summary: This paper establishes the fundamental limits for distinguishing between two quantum dynamical processes described by Lindbladians. It introduces the Lindbladian Stein exponent, which quantifies the rate of distinguishability based on relative entropy. The results reveal that the required measurement protocol depends critically on the available resources, such as total time and the minimum temporal resolution.
main_problem: The paper investigates the fundamental limits of distinguishing between two quantum Markovian dynamics, generated by Lindbladians, by analyzing the optimal type-II error probability.
main_result: The distinguishability is characterized by the Lindbladian Stein exponent, which relates the error decay rate to the largest instantaneous increase of the quantum relative entropy.
method: The analysis uses adaptive quantum hypothesis testing protocols involving sequential evolution steps and intermediate quantum controls, drawing connections to quantum Stein lemmas.
model_or_system: The system involves an auxiliary quantum system evolving under two competing Lindbladian generators, $L_1$ and $L_2$, modeling memoryless quantum dynamics.
key_observables: Type-I and Type-II error probabilities ($\alpha,  eta$), the Lindbladian Stein exponent ($\gamma$), and the optimal error probability $ eta_{\epsilon, t}$.
important_parameters: Total exposure time ($t$), minimum resolution time ($s_{\min}$), and the type-I tolerance ($\epsilon$).
main_assumptions: The dynamics are assumed to be quantum Markovian and time-homogeneous; the analysis considers adaptive protocols with arbitrary instantaneous controls.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the adaptive discrimination protocol, showing the sequence of evolution steps and control channels, and comparing error regimes based on transition rates.
paper_structure: The paper develops the characterization of the Stein exponent, establishes algebraic criteria for its finiteness, and analyzes three distinct regimes (finite exponent, zero error at positive resolution time, and vanishing error requiring $s_{\min} 	o 0$).
why_interesting: This work provides rigorous, quantitative tools (the Stein exponent) to measure how well one can distinguish between different physical processes (dissipative dynamics) using quantum measurements, which is fundamental for quantum process tomography and characterization.
